title: Albert Glenny's advice on chords
summary: Glenny told him a chord is right if the whole band plays it together; conflict arises when players differ.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Here's something I want you to... Even if I have to interrupt your train of thought. There was one nice little thing you told me about once when you worked with Albert Glenny. He told you that pick out a good man to watch and then ask him questions and things like that. Do you remember? What was that he said to you once? Something about... Well, yeah, well... What was some advice he gave you?

Well, the older men had all kind of things. I mean, I don't so well remember that answer. But one thing he did tell me... We were talking about chords one night, you see. And he says, this is one thing about music. He said, D minor might be the right chord. It might be the right chord. He says, but if everybody in the band would make A7, we'll say. But they make it together, then it's the right chord. He says, but where it becomes a bad chord is if two is making D minor and the other fellow is making A7. Then you got a conflict in music. He says, but you go... If they all make B flat and they make it together, that's the right chord. Well, I mean, he had a point there, you see. Because music in itself, in its effect, is the harmony that's balanced against the notes. I mean, if everybody make B flat, it's a perfect chord. But if this fellow make B and the other fellow make G and E make A, well, you got a perfect disc chord there, you know. One of those kind of things.
